title: Event-Driven vs. Scheduled Batch: The Decision Path
purpose: Branch the decision between an event-driven pattern and a scheduled-batch pattern based on reaction latency, durability requirement, and replay need.
accessibleSummary: A root question asks whether the business must react within seconds of an event. If no, the path leads to a scheduled/interval pipeline. If yes, a second question asks whether the event itself is durable state that must be retained, branching to an event-driven pattern with a durable Eventhouse cold path versus a lightweight Activator-only notification pattern. A third question on the durable branch asks whether replay is required, branching to an idempotent replay design versus a simple durable log with no replay contract.
longDescription: This is a top-down branching decision tree, not a linear flow. It starts from the real architectural fork this topic is about: does the business need to react to an event within seconds, or is a scheduled or interval-based pipeline sufficient? If latency tolerance allows minutes-to-hours, a scheduled/interval Data Factory pipeline is the simpler, cheaper choice, since Fabric pipeline schedules and interval-based schedules already cover that case without adding event infrastructure. If sub-second-to-seconds reaction is required, the path moves to Activator-driven event evaluation, and a second question determines whether the event itself is durable business state that must be retained and queried later, or a transient signal that only needs to trigger an action. A durable-state answer leads to the full event-driven pattern with an Eventhouse cold path; a transient-signal answer leads to a lighter Activator-only notification pattern with no cold-path storage. On the durable-state branch, a third question asks whether replay is required — if yes, the design must add an explicit idempotency key and dead-letter/replay procedure; if no, a straightforward durable log without a replay contract is sufficient.

nodes.label: Must the business react within seconds?
nodes.detail: The first branching decision is whether the business process genuinely needs to act on an event within seconds of it occurring, or whether a periodic check is acceptable. This is not a technology question — it is a requirement question that determines whether event infrastructure is justified at all.
nodes.whyItMatters: Event-driven infrastructure (Eventstream, Real-Time hub, Activator, Eventhouse) has real setup and operational cost; a scheduled pipeline is simpler and cheaper when nothing downstream actually consumes sub-minute freshness.

inputs: Business SLA for reacting to the triggering condition
Cost tolerance for continuous evaluation vs. periodic checks
processing: Identify the actual downstream consumer of the reaction and its real freshness need
Compare against what a scheduled or interval-based pipeline can deliver
outputs: A latency requirement in seconds/minutes/hours that determines the next branch
drill.example: A fraud-review team needs to block a high-value order within seconds of it being placed — that is a seconds-scale requirement, not a batch one.
controls: Document the actual business SLA before choosing infrastructure
Avoid defaulting to event-driven because it feels more modern
failureModes: Building event infrastructure for a report that is only reviewed once a day

nodes.label: Use a scheduled or interval pipeline
nodes.summary: Minutes-to-hours latency is fine — a Data Factory pipeline schedule covers it.
nodes.detail: Fabric pipelines can be run on demand, on a time-based schedule (up to 20 schedules per pipeline, each with a required start and end date), or with interval-based schedules (currently preview) that inject window-start/window-end parameters for time-sliced incremental processing. This is the simpler, cheaper answer when sub-minute reaction is not actually required.
nodes.whyItMatters: Choosing this path avoids the operational overhead of event infrastructure when it buys nothing the business actually needs — schedule sprawl and empty runs are a real cost, but so is over-engineering an event-driven system nobody needed.

evidence.note: A pipeline run can be started on demand, on a time-based schedule (up to 20 schedules per pipeline, each requiring start/end dates), or from an event trigger; interval-based schedules (preview) inject window-start/window-end parameters for time-sliced processing.

processing: Configure a time-based or interval-based schedule on the pipeline
Set required start/end dates (schedules have no open-ended option)
Pass schedule-sourced parameters into the pipeline run
outputs: Predictable, scheduled pipeline runs with bounded concurrency
drill.example: A daily sales-summary pipeline runs on a fixed 2am schedule with an end date set five years out; no event infrastructure is needed because nothing downstream reads it before morning.
controls: Up to 20 schedules per pipeline for multiple cadences
Interval schedules for time-sliced incremental loads
failureModes: Interval-based schedules (preview) cannot be edited/enabled/disabled after creation and lack backfill, limiting production windowed-load use

nodes.label: Is the event durable business state?
nodes.summary: Second question: must the event be retained and queried later, or is it just a trigger?
nodes.detail: Given seconds-scale reaction is required, the next question is whether the event itself represents state the business needs to retain and query later (an order, a sensor reading, a transaction) or whether it is a transient signal only meaningful as a trigger (a heartbeat, a threshold crossing that only needs to fire an alert once).
nodes.whyItMatters: This determines whether a cold, durable path (Eventhouse/OneLake) is architecturally required, or whether an Activator-only notification pattern is sufficient and cheaper to run.

inputs: Whether any downstream process needs to query this event's history later
Whether the event has intrinsic business value beyond triggering an action
processing: Ask whether losing the event after the action fires would cause real data loss
Ask whether audit, replay, or historical analytics needs to reference this event later
outputs: A durable-state branch or a transient-signal branch
drill.example: An order.created event is durable business state (it must be queryable for months); a CPU-threshold-crossed heartbeat used only to page an operator is transient.
controls: Distinguish state-carrying events from pure signals during event contract design
failureModes: Treating a transient signal as durable state and over-building storage for it
Treating durable state as transient and losing it after the alert fires

nodes.label: Activator-only notification pattern
nodes.summary: Lightweight: evaluate and act, no durable cold-path storage.
nodes.detail: When the event is a transient signal rather than durable state, the architecture only needs Eventstream routing into Real-Time hub and an Activator rule that fires the action — no Eventhouse ingestion or OneLake mirror is required, since there is nothing worth retaining once the action has fired.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the cheaper, simpler event-driven pattern; adding an unnecessary cold path for signals with no lasting business value is pure operational overhead.

inputs: Transient signal routed through Eventstream/Real-Time hub
processing: Activator rule evaluates the condition
Rule fires its action (notification, job trigger, Power Automate flow)
No cold-path ingestion configured
outputs: Fired action only; no durable record retained
drill.example: A capacity-threshold-crossed signal pages an on-call engineer via Power Automate; once the page is sent there is no requirement to query that specific crossing again next month.
controls: Confirm no compliance or audit requirement exists before skipping the cold path
Revisit if the signal later gains business value
failureModes: A signal quietly becomes business-critical and the missing durable history is discovered only during an incident review

nodes.label: Full event-driven pattern with Eventhouse cold path
nodes.summary: Hot path for immediate action plus a durable Eventhouse/OneLake cold path.
nodes.detail: When the event is durable business state and sub-second-to-seconds reaction is required, the full pattern applies: Eventstream routes into Real-Time hub, which forks into an Activator hot path for immediate action and an Eventhouse cold path for durable, queryable history mirrored to OneLake.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the pattern this topic's architecture diagram visualises end to end — the branch that justifies the full event-driven investment because both the reaction-time and the durability requirements are real.

evidence.note: Real-Time Intelligence is described as a complete end-to-end solution for event-driven and streaming scenarios, covering ingestion through automated actions.

inputs: Durable event routed through Eventstream/Real-Time hub
processing: Fork to Activator for immediate action
Fork to Eventhouse for durable, indexed ingestion
Mirror Eventhouse data to OneLake for cross-workload query
outputs: Immediate action plus a durable, replayable event history
drill.example: An order.created event triggers a fraud-check alert via Activator while independently landing in an Eventhouse table for compliance queries six months later.
controls: Both paths must be provisioned and tested independently, since they are separate subscriptions
Retention and caching policy sized to the required query window
failureModes: Building the hot path first and treating the cold path as an afterthought, producing the notification-as-state risk

nodes.label: Is replay of failed/delayed events required?
nodes.summary: Third question, on the durable branch: does the design need a replay contract?
nodes.detail: Given the durable event-driven pattern applies, the remaining question is whether the business requires the ability to reprocess an event after a downstream failure (replay) or accepts that a failed action is simply logged and handled manually.
nodes.whyItMatters: Replay is not free: it requires an explicit idempotency key so a resubmitted event does not duplicate its original side effect. Skipping this question is how teams end up with the trigger-storm and duplicate-load risks called out on the architecture diagram.

inputs: Business tolerance for a permanently lost action on downstream failure
Compliance/audit requirement to guarantee eventual processing
processing: Determine whether a missed action requires guaranteed eventual reprocessing
Weigh the cost of building an idempotent replay path against manual recovery
outputs: A replay-required branch or a no-replay branch
drill.example: A payment-settlement event must always eventually process, even after a downstream outage — that requires replay. A dashboard-refresh trigger does not — a missed refresh is caught on the next event.
controls: Classify each event type's replay requirement explicitly during design, not after an incident
failureModes: No replay path exists and a downstream outage causes silent, permanent data loss for events that needed guaranteed processing

nodes.label: Idempotent replay + dead-letter design
nodes.summary: Add an explicit idempotency key and dead-letter/replay procedure.
nodes.detail: The design must add an idempotency key enforced on any write that could be replayed, plus a dead-letter/replay procedure that resubmits failed events from the durable Eventhouse history back through Real-Time hub. This is the pattern this topic's architecture diagram shows as its feedback edge.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without the idempotency key, replay itself becomes a data-integrity risk — the exact anti-pattern called out on the architecture diagram (a replay duplicating a load).

inputs: Durable Eventhouse history as the replay source
processing: Detect failure and route the event to a dead-letter record
Enforce an idempotency key on the resubmitted write
Resubmit through Real-Time hub for re-evaluation
outputs: Reliable eventual processing with no duplicate side effects
drill.example: A settlement event that failed due to a downstream outage is replayed from Eventhouse history; the idempotency key on the settlement write ensures the second attempt updates, not duplicates, the ledger entry.
controls: Idempotency key design (natural key, not a generated retry id)
failureModes: Idempotency key derived from a retry attempt id instead of the business event id, defeating its purpose

nodes.label: Durable log, no replay contract
nodes.summary: Land the durable history but do not build a formal replay path.
nodes.detail: When replay is not required, the Eventhouse cold path still provides durable history for audit and analytics, but the design does not need to invest in an automated replay/dead-letter procedure — a failed hot-path action is logged and, if needed, corrected manually by referencing the durable history.
nodes.whyItMatters: This keeps the design honest about scope: not every durable event needs an automated replay contract, and building one unnecessarily adds idempotency-key overhead with no corresponding requirement.

inputs: Failed hot-path action, logged but not auto-replayed
processing: Log the failure with enough context to investigate manually
Leave reprocessing, if ever needed, as a manual, ad hoc query against Eventhouse history
outputs: Auditable durable history; no automated replay pipeline
drill.example: A dashboard-refresh trigger occasionally fails; the durable Eventhouse log lets an engineer confirm what happened, but no automated replay is built because a missed refresh self-corrects on the next event.
controls: Revisit this decision if the event type's business criticality changes
failureModes: Business criticality of the event grows over time and nobody revisits the no-replay decision

walkthrough.title: 1. Start with the reaction-time requirement
walkthrough.explanation: Ask whether the business genuinely needs to react within seconds of the event. This is the root branch that decides whether event infrastructure is justified at all.

walkthrough.title: 2a. No — a scheduled or interval pipeline is enough
walkthrough.explanation: If minutes-to-hours latency is acceptable, a Data Factory time-based or interval-based schedule is the simpler, cheaper answer — stop here.

walkthrough.title: 2b. Yes — now ask whether the event is durable state
walkthrough.explanation: Given seconds-scale reaction is required, the next branch is whether the event is business state worth retaining, or a transient trigger signal.

walkthrough.title: 3a. Transient signal — Activator-only pattern
walkthrough.explanation: If the event has no lasting value once acted on, a lightweight Activator-only pattern with no cold-path storage is sufficient.

walkthrough.title: 3b. Durable state — the full event-driven pattern
walkthrough.explanation: If the event must be retained and queried later, the full pattern applies: Activator hot path plus Eventhouse/OneLake cold path, as shown in this topic's architecture diagram.

walkthrough.title: 4. On the durable branch — is replay required?
walkthrough.explanation: Ask whether a failed hot-path action must be guaranteed to eventually process, or whether manual recovery from the durable log is acceptable.

walkthrough.title: 5a. Yes — build idempotent replay and dead-lettering
walkthrough.explanation: Guaranteed eventual processing requires an explicit idempotency key and a dead-letter/replay procedure, matching the feedback edge on the architecture diagram.

walkthrough.title: 5b. No — durable log without a replay contract
walkthrough.explanation: If manual recovery is acceptable, keep the durable history for audit but skip building an automated replay pipeline you don't need.
